obtained.how: the university repository's own copy: University of Alberta ERA (ualberta.scholaris.ca), reached from doi:10.7939/r3-9pt7-5j74; a National Library of Canada microfiche scan (172 pages) with NO text layer (getsrc reported scanned: true). Read on the page images (findin --image / PyMuPDF renders): abstract, contents, chapter 3 methods, results and discussion, chapter 4 methods and results, chapter 5 methods, Appendix Table 6

bibliography.checked_against: the National Library microfiche form and the thesis approval page (PDF pp. 1, 4)
bibliography.note: James Stephen Diana, 'An energy budget for northern pike (Esox lucius) in Lac Ste. Anne, Alberta', Ph.D. thesis, University of Alberta, 1979 (supervisor W. C. Mackay; approved May 30, 1979). The DOI is a repository (DataCite) DOI, hence 'not found at Crossref'. Printed page = PDF page − 12 in the body.

claims.claim: in Lac Ste. Anne pike moved more than 5 m in only 16 % of 5-minute intervals in summer overall: 22 % around sunrise, 17 % by day, 21 % around sunset and 2 % at night
claims.location: p. 85 (PDF p. 97), Table 14; methods p. 81–83 (PDF pp. 93–95)
claims.conditions: ultrasonic telemetry of six pike (46–59 cm SL, 0.94–2.2 kg; Table 13) from March to July 1978; positions triangulated every 5 min for ≥ 1 h; 'inactive' = movement < 5 m, the minimum that could be detected accurately (about 2 m in winter to 5 m in summer); sunrise = ½ h before to 1 h after sunrise, sunset = 1 h before to ½ h after sunset; summer n = 651 intervals
claims.note: Winter was similar: 23, 19, 35 and 2 %, overall 21 %; no significant summer–winter difference (chi-square 2.71, P = 0.10).

claims.claim: Diana studied 1,290 pike in Lac Ste. Anne
claims.conditions: gill-netted on 26 occasions, March 1976 – September 1978; diet table pooled by month over the years

claims.location: p. 62 (PDF p. 74), Results; p. 63 (PDF p. 75), Table 10 ('Empty 611 (47)')
claims.quote: occurring in 29 to 62% of the fish sampled each month
claims.conditions: months sampled: May, June, July, August, September, October, January, March (29 % in October, 62 % in January)
claims.note: Diana notes that small-mesh gill nets caught a higher share of empty pike, and excluded them from the ration analysis (p. 65).

claims.quote: The most common meal consisted of 1 item
claims.conditions: Figure 6, n = 665 stomachs with food: 61 % held one item, 20 % two, 8 % three, ≤ 2 % each of more; mean fish per stomach about 2 every month except October (5.24, young-of-year perch)

claims.claim: meals came 2.7–2.8 days apart in summer and about 25 days apart in winter
claims.conditions: time between meals (days) estimated from the share of empty stomachs and the time until ingested weight can no longer be estimated (B′: 30 h in summer, 8 d in winter); winter 25 d for both sexes; data pooled 1976–78; pike from small-mesh nets excluded

claims.claim: gastric evacuation slowed from 48 h in summer to 12 days in winter
claims.location: p. 62 (PDF p. 74), Results; abstract p. v (PDF p. 6); methods p. 61 (PDF p. 73)
claims.quote: the gastric evacuation time (B) was 48 hours in summer, 12 days in winter.
claims.conditions: laboratory: adult pike starved, then force-fed 2-year-old yellow perch, six fish per temperature, sacrificed at intervals; experiments at 2 and 16 °C (methods) — the abstract says 2 and 14 °C
claims.note: Lac Ste. Anne runs near 16 °C (14–20) from May to October and near 1–2 °C from November to April.

claims.claim: in summer, 3-year-old pike of 0.9–1.2 kg ate about 1.0–1.6 % of their body weight a day
claims.source_value: Diana gives rations in energy, not %BW: summer daily ration 11.4 kcal/kg/day (males) and 17.4 kcal/kg/day (females), for all pike pooled by sex (Table 12). 3-year-olds weighed 0.83–1.19 kg from May to October (Appendix Table 6). Converting with his own perch values (Table 9: 0.237 dry matter × 4.5 kcal/g dry ≈ 1.07 kcal/g wet) gives ≈ 1.1 and 1.6 %BW/d — a project conversion
claims.location: p. 68 (PDF p. 80), Table 12; p. 60 (PDF p. 72), Table 9; p. 156 (PDF p. 168), Appendix Table 6
claims.conditions: Table 12 units: meal size kcal/kg, ration kcal/kg/day; Appendix Table 6 gives 3-year-old body weights (g) by month: May M 893, F 831; July M 987, F 1012; Sept M 1034, F 1151; Oct M 1069, F 1191
claims.note: The arithmetic holds (11.4 / 1.07 = 10.7 g/kg/d = 1.07 %; 17.4 / 1.07 = 16.3 g/kg/d = 1.63 %), but the ration results (Tables 12 and 16, Appendix Table 6) are all in kcal and print no %BW/d figure: write 'about 11–17 kcal/kg/d (≈ 1.0–1.6 %BW/d, project conversion with Diana's perch energy density)'. The rations in Table 12 are for all pike, not only 3-year-olds (chapter 5 applies them to 3-year-olds, p. 92). Monthly rations range widely, e.g. June females 30.9 kcal/kg/d (≈ 2.9 %BW/d).

claims.claim: in summer, females ate 1.5–2.3 times as much as males
claims.source_value: 1.5 times in summer, 2.3 times in winter
claims.quote: the mean female ration was 1.5 (summer) to 2.3 (winter) times the male ration
claims.conditions: ratio of mean daily rations (kcal/kg/day); higher female rations came from larger meals, feeding frequency being similar
claims.note: The sentence places the whole range in summer; 2.3 is the winter ratio.

claims.claim: about 65 % of the year's energy gain came between May and July
claims.source_value: about 65 % of the year's ration (food energy eaten) was ingested from May 1 to August 1, by 3-year-old pike; the discussion calls it 'annual energy accumulation' but Figure 7 plots kcal eaten
claims.location: p. 69 (PDF p. 81), Results; p. 75 (PDF p. 87), Discussion; p. 71 (PDF p. 83), Figure 7
claims.quote: About 65% of the total annual ration was ingested from May 1 to August 1.
claims.conditions: monthly ration = daily ration × mean weight of 3-year-olds × days in month, for one year beginning in May
claims.note: Table 16 (p. 98, PDF p. 110) agrees: May 1–July 31 ingestion 1,130 kcal (male) and 1,813 kcal (female) of annual totals 1,742 and 2,774 kcal (summer + winter rows) = 65 %. 'Energy gain' reads as growth; it is intake. Write 'about 65 % of the year's food was eaten between May and July'.

notes: Scanned thesis without a text layer: every quote is off a page image (quote_from 'image'). The paper's '(thesis read by a sub-researcher)' tag can now go. Other values: diet by number mostly yellow perch, then spottail shiner, burbot, white sucker, whitefish, walleye; one pike in a pike stomach (August); perch were about half the energy intake, suckers and burbot more by energy than by number; rations ~20 times higher in summer than winter; spawning fast from mid-April to May; three replicate June 1978 samples gave male 9.6 and 8.4 and female 11.1, 12.0 and 12.7 kcal/kg/day; maximum swimming speeds 17–42 cm/s; 3-year-old females allotted 47 % of assimilated energy to maintenance, 25 % to growth, 28 % to reproduction (abstract). The paper's separate Diana (1983) caveat (field rations probably inaccurate) is not in this thesis.
